Article Title: Steve Jobs said it wouldn't work, but with Apple's first touchscreen MacBook now here, John Ternus says you've gotta touch it to believe it
Article Text:
The first touchscreen Mac arrives, 16 years after Steve Jobs said it wouldn’t work.

Apple kept saying no, and nobody else quite proved it wrong

Touch could only come if it cost the Mac nothing

Jobs would still mind the tired arms, and Apple knows it

For 16 years, Apple had an answer ready whenever someone asked about a touchscreen Mac, and the answer was always some version of no.Steve Jobs gave it first, with the most theatre. Tim Cook gave it with kitchen appliances, and Phil Schiller with user studies. In 2021, Apple's then hardware engineering chief, John Ternus, told The Wall Street Journal's Joanna Stern that the Mac was built around the keyboard and trackpad, adding: "We haven't really felt a reason to change that. "Apple has now found one.The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a mouthful even by Apple's standards, so I'll call it the touchscreen MacBook Pro from here on. It is the first Mac that responds to a finger on its screen, and also the first MacBook with an OLED panel, which, as Apple tells it, is the very reason touch could happen at all.When Wired asked Ternus, now nearly two months into the CEO job, whether Apple was about to break its oldest Mac taboo, he kept it brief: "Who knew?" On X, he was a little less brief, writing that Apple was "glowing with excitement" over the new MacBook Pro and that "you've gotta touch it to believe it." With the glowing Apple logo back on the lid, the pun was almost certainly intended.That is quite a turn for someone who, five years ago, couldn't see a reason to change the Mac at all, and Apple can expect some ribbing for it.The reversal is also typical of how the company works. Apple's "never" has usually carried an unwritten condition, roughly "until we can do it in a way we like," and no product has taken longer to get past it than the touchscreen Mac.Jobs set the tone in October 2010, barely ten months after he had introduced the iPad. Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical, he argued on stage. Reaching up to a laptop screen made for a nice demo, but Apple's own testing showed fatigue set in quickly, and after long enough, "your arm wants to fall off." Touch belonged on horizontal surfaces, which is why MacBooks got big glass trackpads instead.Cook made a similar case two years later. Asked on a 2012 earnings call whether tablets and laptops would eventually merge, he likened the idea to combining "a toaster and a refrigerator," suggesting the result would please nobody. Microsoft released its first Surface tablets that same year, alongside a version of Windows rebuilt around touch.Then came Schiller. In 2015, Apple's marketing chief laid out a broader theory of the product line to journalist Steven Levy: every Apple device is essentially a computer behind a sheet of glass, and each gets the interface that suits how it is used. Reaching over a fixed keyboard to poke a screen was uncomfortable, he argued, and macOS was built for the precision of a pointer, with tiny buttons and dense menus that fingers would fumble.A year later, Apple did put touch on the MacBook Pro, just not on the display. The Touch Bar sat above the keyboard, and Schiller said the company had tested touchscreen Macs internally and come away convinced its instincts were right. The Touch Bar itself didn't last. Physical function keys returned in 2021, and the strip was gone from the lineup by 2023.Stern, for her part, kept asking. When she put the question to software chief Craig Federighi at the Journal's Tech Live event in October 2022, he replied "Who's to say?" and the panel broke into laughter. By June 2025, Federighi and marketing head Greg Joswiak were meeting it with laughter alone. Going back through her archive on X this week, Stern noted that Apple's replies had slowly drifted from a flat "nope" to evasive laughter.In hindsight, that was about as close to a yes as Apple ever gets.Elsewhere, in the Windows world, touchscreen laptops became routine long ago. Machines with screens you can tap, and often fold back into a tablet, have sat on store shelves for well over a decade without ever being short of buyers. A generation raised on phones and tablets expects every screen to respond to touch, and plenty of laptops happily oblige.Selling them, though, isn't the same as settling the argument, and Microsoft's own history shows it. Windows 8 rebuilt the PC around touch, and the backlash was strong enough that the Start button came back within a year. Windows 10 restored the familiar desktop, Windows 11 quietly dropped the dedicated tablet mode, and the company that bet hardest on touchscreen laptops has spent the decade since easing touch into the background. Part of the reason is that the trade-offs never went away. A touchscreen still tends to mean a glossier panel, more weight and shorter battery life, and with most apps never rethought for fingers, people were rarely given a good reason to reach for the screen.Apple, meanwhile, was edging closer from the other side. The iPad picked up trackpad support in 2020 and a far more Mac-like iPadOS last year, complete with resizable windows and a menu bar. The Mac, in turn, had been running iPhone and iPad apps since its move to Apple silicon, apps built for fingers that never felt quite right under a cursor.By January 2023, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman was reporting that Apple had a touchscreen MacBook Pro in the works, originally pencilled in for 2025. That date slipped, and for good reason. Apple had clearly decided a touchscreen Mac was coming; what it hadn't worked out yet was how to add one without giving anything up.Ternus's explanation for the timing is the most revealing part of this story. Apple, he told Wired, needed to reach a point where adding touch didn't make the MacBook Pro worse in any way: not heavier, not thicker. Anything earlier would have meant a compromise on the company's most expensive laptop.The OLED panel is what made the maths work. The touch sensor is built directly into the display rather than laid on top as a separate layer, so it adds neither bulk nor noticeable lag, and because OLED needs no backlight, the lid slims down too. The 16-inch model now weighs about 1.8kg, roughly 300 grams less than before, while the 14-inch drops to around 1.36kg. Both are marginally thinner, and slimmer borders stretch the screens to 14.2 and 16.3 inches.Apple calls it the best laptop display in the world, and the numbers support the claim. The tandem OLED panel stacks two light-emitting layers to hit 2,000 nits in both HDR and everyday SDR use, with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, a refresh rate that moves between 10Hz and 120Hz, and colour that spans both P3 and Adobe RGB.For photographers, and I count myself among them, that last detail will matter more than any tap or swipe.The smaller decisions tell you how seriously Apple took the ergonomics argument it once made against itself. The hinge has been redesigned to keep the display steady under a finger, though early demo footage still shows a slight bounce on a firm tap. The cooling system now pushes warm air away from the panel so it doesn't feel hot to the touch. Even the webcam has been considered, with stabilisation that smooths the video feed when you tap the screen mid-call.Software is where Schiller's old objections have been dealt with most directly. macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn't throw out the desktop the way Windows 8 did with its tiles. The menu bar and windows look as they always have, but in the demos Wired saw, menu items and the little traffic-light buttons grew as a finger reached them, so a tap lands where it should. Looking back, the rounder buttons and roomier menu bar that came with Liquid Glass were clearly groundwork.Apps that haven't been updated still respond, because macOS simply translates a tap into a click, and the Dynamic Island crosses over from the iPhone as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. Apple's own apps go further, with a multi-touch keyboard in Logic Pro and pinch-to-zoom on a cut in Final Cut Pro, while apps from Lightroom and DaVinci Resolve to Blender and Microsoft Office are lining up support.Apple's footnote is less eager. Those apps arrive later this year, and as with the iPhone Duo, where many apps are still being updated for the folding screen, it may be a while before touch feels at home across the Mac.The pricing makes the intended audience clear. The 14-inch model with M5 Pro starts at Rs 3,49,900 in India and the 16-inch at Rs 4,09,900, while the M5 Max versions begin at Rs 5,49,900 and Rs 5,89,900. In the US, the two start at $2,899 and $3,399, and a fully specced 16-inch model climbs all the way to $14,549.Joswiak's case, as he put it to Wired, is that Apple's professional users already own an iPad and an iPhone, and that a younger generation of creators simply expects a screen to respond to touch. The MacBook Air and iMac don't get it, and Ternus, predictably, wouldn't say whether they ever will. Apple has made a neat case for what touch can do for colourists, musicians and developers, but the harder sell will come if it ever reaches the MacBook Air, where Apple will face the same question Windows laptops never quite answered for everyday buyers: why anyone needs to reach for the screen at all.Nobody is being pushed into it, either. The regular 14-inch MacBook Pro, refreshed only a day earlier with Apple's newer M6 chip, stays on the shelves without a touchscreen. That leaves buyers with a slightly odd choice: the touchscreen model gets the better display, while the one without it gets the newer processor.Which brings us to Jobs.It's easy to picture him furious, and plenty of longtime Apple fans will insist this would never have happened on his watch. I'm not so sure.Jobs said a lot of things on stage that Apple later quietly undid. He maintained the company had no interest in making a phone, right up until the iPhone. He waved off video on the iPod until the hardware could handle it. In 2007, he said that if you see a stylus, "they blew it," and Apple now sells a Pencil that works with the iPad and the new iPhone Duo. In almost every case, his no was aimed at the version of an idea that existed at the time.The touchscreen laptop of 2010 fits that pattern. It was usually a touch layer added to an ordinary laptop screen, running software built for a mouse, and his complaint about holding an arm up to it was fair. Sixteen years on, nobody has offered a convincing answer to it, and Apple isn't trying to: the trackpad hasn't shrunk, and Ternus still describes the Mac as an indirect input device first. Touch here is for the moments when reaching out is quicker than steering a cursor, whether that's nudging a colour wheel, playing a chord, pinching into a photo or tapping a Live Activity.So what would Jobs say? He would probably still tell you your arm will get tired, and he would be right. Then he would likely ask whether the screen underneath was the best Apple had ever made, whether touch had cost the machine a single gram or millimetre, and whether macOS still felt like macOS.This MacBook Pro has an answer to each of those, and getting there took 16 years. For a company whose co-founder once called touchscreen laptops "ergonomically terrible," taking that long to say yes might be the most Jobs-like thing it has done in a while.
Article Summary: The first touchscreen Mac arrives, 16 years after Steve Jobs said it wouldn't work. It is the first Mac that responds to a finger on its screen, and also the first MacBook with an OLED panel. Apple can expect some ribbing for it, and the reversal is also typical of how the company works.

Article Title: First ever AI supercomputer is heading to the Moon: What it means for humanity’s future
Article Text:
Testing next-gen computational hardware in deep space is viewed as a vital step to support future human habitation and long-term economic activity across the lunar frontier even as Nasa pushes closer to returning astronauts to the moon under its Artemis program.

Edge computing on Moon and what is so special about his computer

Borrowing proven navigation tech from Mars

A historic computing milestone is set to reach the lunar surface later this year as California-based space company Astrolab prepares to launch its uncrewed moon rover, FLIP, equipped with Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4. The launch will mark the first time high-performance computing, graphics processing units (GPUs) and artificial intelligence (AI) experiments are deployed and tested directly on the moon.The uncrewed rover will touch down near the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1 (Griffin-1). Astrolab is one of two private firms selected by NASA to develop a drivable rover for Artemis, as per Space.com.“We're sending the first supercomputer from HPE to the lunar surface later this year, doing the first GPU on the moon [and the] first AI experiments on the moon. They're breaking new ground, and they're ahead of the curve,” said Jaret Matthews, founder and CEO of Astrolab, during a media event at company headquarters earlier this month.To handle the harsh space environment, HPE’s Spaceborne Computer-4 has been engineered as a lightweight, compact, fanless and self-contained system. Its core features include a low-power 64-bit CPU paired with an integrated GPU, solid-state drives (SSDs) by memory specialist KIOXIA, and heat-conductive aluminium housing connected directly to FLIP’s cooling system, with energy supplied by the rover’s combination of onboard solar cells and batteries.However, the primary technical objective of the system is proving that it can survive the grueling environmental extremes of the lunar south pole. Matthews explained: “We have to design for a full year on the lunar surface. So that means surviving multiple lunar nights, upwards of 150 hours of complete darkness where we're not receiving energy or warmth from the sun.”Matthews noted that the rover must operate autonomously for long stretches when astronauts are absent: “We're having to develop a semi-autonomous platform that will spend many months [and] travel hundreds of kilometers.”Beyond durability, the supercomputer will actively process visual feeds captured during transit, conduct autonomous observations, assist in terrain analysis and run lunar mapping tasks. HPE noted in a statement that “an AI services container will demonstrate reliable deployment of scalable AI service applications on the moon,” laying the groundwork for how future crewed missions might harness AI in deep space.As the moon lacks a global positioning system (GPS), navigation represents a serious technical hurdle for surface exploration. To solve this, Astrolab is leveraging software originally designed for Mars exploration by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), where Matthews previously worked.“One of the experiments [that will be] running on the spaceborne computer on the moon is a localization software experiment from JPL. It has been used on Mars, and this will be the first time it's used on the moon,” Matthews added.The system relies on a machine learning algorithm that cross-references onboard map data with real-time visual observations of the surrounding landscape. By matching observed landmarks against its internal memory, the rover can establish its exact coordinates on the map and steer clear of treacherous craters without needing GPS signals.
Article Summary: HPE's Spaceborne Computer-4 is set to reach the lunar surface later this year. It will be the first time high-performance computing, graphics processing units (GPUs) and artificial intelligence (AI) experiments are deployed and tested directly on the moon. The uncrewed rover, FLIP, will touch down near the lunar south pole.

Article Title: In 2015, a Georgia crash injured an Uber driver who later sued Snapchat over its speed filter; a decade later, Snap settles even after CEO Evan Spiegel defended the feature under oath
Article Text:
In pic: Snapchat CEO Evan Spiegel

What happened in the Georgia crash

Why the lawsuit targeted Snapchat’s design

What Snapchat CEO Evan Spiegel said under oath

“From my perspective, Snap was thoughtful about the design and release of the speed filter,”

“The Parties’ dispute was resolved in an amicable manner, pursuant to a confidential agreement, and no Party admitted any liability.”

Snap has settled a lawsuit over Snapchat’s speed filter. The case followed a September 2015 crash in Georgia that left Uber driver Wentworth Maynard with a permanent brain injury. His lawsuit alleged that the feature, which let users display their traveling speed on photos and videos, encouraged the teenage driver who struck his car to accelerate.According to a report by Bloomberg Businessweek, Snap settled the lawsuit this month, before jury selection, which was scheduled for November 2. The confidential agreement ended a decade of litigation, during which chief executive Evan Spiegel defended the filter’s design under oath. Snap disputed that Snapchat was being used when the collision occurred, and the settlement included no admission of liability.On September 10, 2015, 18-year-old Christal McGee was driving three co-workers home from a restaurant in Lovejoy, Georgia, when her Mercedes struck Maynard’s Mitsubishi on Tara Boulevard.Passenger Heather McCarty said McGee was using Snapchat’s speed filter and trying to reach 100 mph to post it.The lawsuit alleged that the Mercedes was travelling at about 107 mph at impact.McGee denied speeding or using Snapchat during the drive. Snap said its activity logs showed she had not opened the app during the period covering the crash. The plaintiffs challenged the logs’ reliability and pointed to missing data.Maynard spent 71 days in medical care, including time in an induced coma. According to Businessweek, his injuries left him unable to work or drive and caused extensive memory loss.Filed in April 2016 in Georgia’s Spalding County State Court, the lawsuit alleged that Snapchat had negligently designed a feature that encouraged dangerous driving.That distinction mattered because Section 230, a federal law, generally shields internet platforms from liability for user-posted content. The Maynards’ lawyers argued that their claim concerned something Snapchat built, rather than something a user published.The filter launched in December 20and warneding against using Snapchat while driving. Court records Bloomberg reviewed contained customer complaints and internal discussions about distracted driving. Snap discontinued the feature in 2021.Spiegel testified in a deposition in autumn 2024 that ad personal created the speed filter. He defended the company’s safeguards and said he had not been personally alerted to customer messages warning of dangerous driving.he said. Asked about regrets, Spiegel said Snap was not in use during this particular crash.In August 2026, Judge Josh Thacker rejected Snap’s request to end the case without a trial. His ruling allowed jurors to consider the evidence; it did not establish the company’s liability.The settlement followed in October. Snap said:

His lawsuit alleged that the feature, which let users display their traveling speed on photos and videos, encouraged the teenage driver who struck his car to accelerate.

Anthropic manager’s five-step advice for junior engineers worried about AI

AI layoffs are hitting entry-level tech jobs the hardest

Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg has stopped asking job candidates to take coding interviews, and his reason is simple: Claude is now better at them. In a blog post on October 27, Rieseberg, who has led engineering for Claude.ai, Cowork and Claude Code Desktop, also shared advice for junior engineers worried about AI eating into their careers, at a time when AI has become the top reason companies give for layoffs.His take is more hopeful than most. Newcomers bring fresh eyes, he argues, and AI has made their impact less dependent on years of experience. The catch is that companies rarely listen to people without status. “The only problem with all that ignorant power: Nobody cares what you think,” he wrote. The upside, he added, is that building something is no longer expensive.Small coding challenges were once a weak but useful signal of how someone would perform on his teams, but Rieseberg says that no longer holds. Handing a candidate a little React task now makes as much sense as quizzing them on assembly, because Claude is better at both. His most impactful builders, he noted, succeed regardless of how they do on such tests.Instead, he is watching relatively new engineers overtake people who are probably better coders and have been around much longer. He calls it “hunger beats tenure”, and says the advice is really for anyone without social capital, status or power, whatever their title.He draws on his own career. At Notion, one of his job interviews asked him to design an offline mode the company considered impossible, partly because it believed CEO Ivan Zhao would never approve the experience. That belief turned out to be wrong, and nobody had bothered to check.First, chase business impact over your backlog. Work out what your company or department is trying to achieve, using your manager’s manager’s goals as a guide. Then pick a radical idea that could sharply improve the odds of hitting those goals, and build a working prototype over a weekend instead of writing product documents and lobbying for a designer’s time.Keep that prototype to one idea. Juniors, he says, often hide “three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones”. Finally, use the outsider’s view. New hires understand users better than veterans do, and they haven’t yet learnt all the reasons something is supposedly impossible.Anthropic itself offers his sharpest example. Staff had grown so used to Claude Code as a command-line tool that it took two relatively new engineers, Anthony Morris and Alice Zhao, to build a working graphical version over one weekend. The first public version shipped about eight days later.The advice lands at an anxious time for freshers. AI was the most cited reason for job cuts in the US in September, behind 21% of all announced layoffs, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, with tech alone accounting for 29% of cuts. Microsoft has offered buyouts to 60,000 employees and Oracle has cut 21,000 jobs. Goldman Sachs now estimates AI could displace up to 9% of US workers, roughly 15 million people, in the coming years.Anthropic is no exception. The company said last week that its share of entry-level technical hires has dropped from nearly 30% to 9% since March 2025, and its IPO filing shows Claude produced more than 90% of contributions to its codebase in September. CEO Dario Amodei warned last year that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years.Not everyone buys the doom. Some economists argue firms are “AI-washing” cuts they would have made anyway, and US unemployment is still hovering around 4.1%.Rieseberg admits he hasn’t yet worked out how to interview for people who build well with AI. For now, he scans resumes and portfolios for small prototypes that show taste, empathy and principled thinking. If anyone has figured out a better way, he wrote, he would love to hear it.
Article Summary: Anthropic has stopped asking job candidates to take coding interviews. Manager Felix Rieseberg says Claude is now better at them. He also shared advice for junior engineers worried about AI eating into their careers. AI was the most cited reason for job cuts in the US in September.

Article Title: Amazon layoffs hit devices and ‌services unit; company's 'early morning' email to laid off employees says: A thorough review of ​our ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

Amazon unveils new lineup of Alexa devices

Amazon's open memo to engineers

Amazon layoffs are back. Ecommerce giant has announced new job cuts. According to a report in Reuters, Amazon is cutting about 250 jobs in its devices and ‌services unit after weeks of product rollouts including new Kindle e-readers and tablet computers. The company reportedly confirmed the job cuts after a Reuters inquiry. "We've made the difficult decision to eliminate a small number ⁠of roles," a spokesperson said. The layoffs will help the company "operate more efficiently and better align with our product roadmap," the statement added.According to the report, quoting a person familiar with the matter, the ​layoffs impact no more than 250 jobs, and are primarily in software development teams. As is the company's custom, text messages and emails were sent to employees early Wednesday morning (October 28). A layoff email, reportedly seen by ​Reuters, was ​from Cherie ⁠Robinson, a human resources vice president in devices and services, saying ​that the company had undergone "a thorough review of ​our ⁠structure" resulting in the need for cuts.In January this year, Amazon announced that it is cutting 16,000 jobs across the company.This announcement came after the e-commerce company laid off 14,000 people in October. During January layoffs, senior VP of People Experience and Technology Beth Galetti told employees that these layoffs were made for “reducing layers, increasing ownership, and removing bureaucracy.” She noted that the reason for the second round of massive layoffs within three months was that several teams in the company hadn’t finished their restructuring. “Some of you might ask if this is the beginning of a new rhythm – where we announce broad reductions every few months. That’s not our plan. But just as we always have, every team will continue to evaluate the ownership, speed, and capacity to invent for customers, and make adjustments as appropriate,” she said.Incidentally, the job cuts in the devices division came on the day Amazon unveiled five new Alexa-powered devices including a redesigned Echo Show 16 smart display and a photo frame with ‌built-in Alexa. The new product launches come as Amazon pushes its latest version of the voice assistant into customers' homes. Amazon is rolling out the devices as it ⁠faces growing competition from rivals including Apple, as well as AI companies such as OpenAI that have hardware ambitions.The Echo Show 16, which has a ​16-inch screen, built-in Fire TV and Amazon's ⁠first Echo Show camera with night vision, ​is priced at $499.99. A new Echo Studio ​speaker with a built-in camera, which lets Alexa recognize objects held up to it and lets users check ​on a room remotely, is priced at $249.99. The new Echo ​Dot is priced at $99.99. The device includes a built-in smart home hub and ‌Wi-Fi ⁠extender for the first time.Echo Time is a bedside clock, priced at $199. According to the company, it uses sleep-sensing technology to wake users during lighter sleep, without a wearable device. The Alexa ​Photo Frame, ​starting at $199.99, ⁠syncs pictures automatically from Amazon Photos.Just a day earlier, Amazon published a memo it shared with engineers in September on its website. Titled: 'Update from Amazon engineering leadership on the role of the developer in the age of AI'; the memo has Amazon engineering leaders revise the role guideline for software development engineers, underscoring what matters most is the outcome, not which tools are used. "We all need to embrace this change and take the time to learn, or we risk being left behind. We’re just seeing the beginning of AI’s effect on software engineering. While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there’s a lot that’s still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice," reads the memo.
Article Summary: Report: Amazon is cutting about 250 jobs in its devices and ‌services unit. The company reportedly confirmed the job cuts after a Reuters inquiry. In January this year, Amazon announced that it is cutting 16,000 jobs across the company. This announcement came after the e-commerce company laid off 14,000 people in October.

Article Title: Reddit now has two homepage feeds: What the new ‘For You’ and ‘Following’ tabs show you
Article Text:
Reddit splits its home feed in two

Reddit has been steering its homepage towards algorithms all year

Reddit is changing what users see the moment they open the app. The platform has split its homepage into two feeds, “For You” and “Following,” a format TikTok made popular, and the new layout is rolling out globally over the next few weeks.Following sticks to posts from subreddits a user has already joined. For You mixes those posts with recommendations based on their interests, including communities they browse but have never subscribed to. Someone who keeps checking r/Silksong without joining it could now find those threads near the top of their home feed.Reddit says the idea is discovery. In a blog post, the company described the new feeds as “a first step in helping drive discovery that leads to something novel and relevant.”Switching between the two takes a tap, and Reddit remembers the last one used. Close the app on Following, and it opens on Following next time.The shift has been building for months. Earlier this year, Reddit announced it would deprecate r/all, the page that surfaced popular posts from across the platform, as part of a push to simplify the site and personalise Home. Recommended posts from outside a user’s subreddits aren’t new either.They simply get their own dedicated space now.The change puts Reddit in line with Instagram, X, Threads and Facebook, all of which lean on “For You”-style feeds. Not every user is on board, though. Some who saw the feature during testing have already complained, and plenty of regulars value Reddit precisely because their feed reflects communities they picked.For them, Old Reddit at old.reddit.com still offers the classic “best,” “hot,” “new,” “rising” and “controversial” sorting. Reddit has said it will limit Old Reddit access for accounts that haven’t used it recently, blaming AI bots, so anyone attached to it should log in soon.
Article Summary: Reddit is changing what users see the moment they open the app. The platform has split its homepage into two feeds, “For You” and “Following” The new layout is rolling out globally over the next few weeks.

Article Title: Starting December, Discord will make some public server messages available on Google Search; here’s who’s included and how to opt out
Article Text:
Which servers and messages are included

Who is included by default

How can members opt out

What can server administrators control

Discord will soon make some public server messages searchable online. In a recent announcement, the company said messages from participating public channels in Discoverable Servers could appear on server web pages and in web search from mid-December 2026. The rollout will be gradual, so the first messages may take several weeks to appear.The change is intended to make community knowledge, including gaming guides and answers to common questions, accessible outside Discord. Administrators can decide which channels participate, while members can control whether their messages appear. The announcement refers to web search generally and does not specifically name Google Search. Private servers, direct messages and group direct messages are excluded.The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers, which include communities listed in Discord’s Server Discovery that anyone can join without an invitation. These servers must have at least 1,000 members, be at least eight weeks old, and meet activity and safety requirements.Only messages sent from mid-December onwards in participating public channels will be eligible.Earlier messages will not be included, regardless of a member’s settings. Discord will label channels whose content may appear on the web.Usernames and avatars will not appear alongside messages on Server Web Pages. Teen users are excluded from the Channel Messages feature and cannot enable it until adulthood.In the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea, the member setting is off by default. Members in these regions must enable it before their messages can appear.Elsewhere, the setting is on by default unless members turn it off. A message can appear only if the server’s administrators also allow the channel to participate.Members can disable sharing through these steps:1. Open User Settings2. Select Data and Privacy.3. Turn off “Show my message content from Discoverable channels on web pages”.The switch applies across every Discoverable Server the member belongs to. Discord began rolling out these controls on October 27, ahead of the message-sharing launch.Turning the setting off later prevents future messages from appearing. Messages shared while it was enabled remain online unless the member deletes them from Discord.Administrators can open Server Settings > Web Presence to select participating channels or exclude all channels. Public channels remain enabled by default if administrators make no changes.Every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page from November 16. If administrators have not created one, Discord will publish a default page using the server’s profile details.Automated Channel Summaries may also begin appearing that day, drawing on conversations from November 16 onwards. These summaries are controlled separately: a member opting out of message sharing does not disable them. Administrators can choose their source channels, curate the summaries, or turn them off entirely.
Article Summary: Discord will soon make some public server messages searchable online. Messages from participating public channels in Discoverable Servers could appear on server web pages and in web search from mid-December 2026. The rollout will be gradual, so the first messages may take several weeks to appear. Administrators can decide which channels participate, while members can control whether their messages appear.

Article Title: Meta AI director Rohit Patel leaves company after eight years; plans startup to take on Microsoft Office and Google Workspace; says adding AI to spreadsheets ‘kills my…’
Article Text:
In pic: Meta's ex-AI director Rohit Patel

What does Ndoc do

Why did Rohit Patel left Meta

When will Ndoc be available

Meta AI director Rohit Patel is leaving the company after eight years. According to a TechCrunch report, the former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc, a startup he is positioning as an AI alternative to Microsoft Office and Google Workspace. He aims to bring analysis, presentations, and underlying data into one workspace, eliminating the need to switch between separate apps.“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” Patel told TechCrunch. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”Ndoc organises work into three connected tabs. Stage displays presentations, dashboards, simulations and small applications. Narrative contains written analysis, citations and generated figures. Model holds the underlying datasets and Python scripts, allowing users to inspect how results were produced.Users can upload data and ask the platform to analyse it and explain the findings. They can also provide context about the intended audience and tone.According to Patel, colleagues can access the shared workspace even without signing up for Ndoc.The emphasis on checking AI output reflects Patel’s work at Meta, where he focused on reinforcement learning, training AI through rewards and trial and error, and evaluating whether its output could be trusted.“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”Patel said his wish to make Ndoc’s document format openly available was partly behind his decision to leave. He believed securing agreement on such a format within Meta would involve input from many people and slow development.Ndoc can export documents as a single “.ndoc.html” file that opens in a browser, according to Patel. He plans to open-source the format so other developers can build compatible applications and users can access their work without depending entirely on Ndoc.The platform uses a mixture of open-source AI models. Patel claims this makes it considerably cheaper to operate than alternatives using more advanced proprietary models.Ndoc has a three-person team and has not raised funding, the report added. Patel said he wanted evidence of customer demand before approaching investors.The startup is running an enterprise pilot and offering an early test version to a limited number of customers via a waiting list. Signing up is free, but customers will pay for usage and tokens, the units AI models use to process information.Patel hopes to release a broader beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year. The company has also built connections to existing workplace tools so customers can import their data.
Article Summary: Rohit Patel is leaving Meta Superintelligence Labs after eight years. He has launched Ndoc, an AI alternative to Microsoft Office and Google Workspace. Ndoc organises work into three connected tabs. Stage displays presentations, dashboards, simulations and small applications. Narrative contains written analysis, citations and generated figures. Model holds underlying datasets and Python scripts.
